title: When Retrieval Lies

post.author: u/strongroom_ursula
post.title: I'm the night archivist at a county record office. At 02:14 our search assistant told a family historian that a widow inherited a mill her husband never owned.

blocks.text: I work nights at the Fenmarrow Record Office, in a search room nobody visits after six. Since the spring, family historians abroad can put questions to our assistant overnight, and it answers from the county's 19th-century estate papers: 1,860 documents cut into 31,400 chunks, each one embedded and also indexed for keyword search. It sends the top 5 chunks to a model, about 40 questions a night. I built it, and I thought I'd built it properly. Every chunk keeps its estate and section as metadata, and the assistant shows them under each answer, so a reader can check the source.

02:14  visitor  who owned Cauldmere Mill in 1871?
02:14  archive  1871. In January Mr Ozias Polkinghorne died, and by his will
                 Cauldmere Mill passed to his widow, Mrs Petronella Polkinghorne,
                 who owned it for life.
                 source: Polkinghorne estate papers > Brackenholt Mill: wills and accounts
02:16  visitor  and after her?
02:16  archive  I can find nothing about that in the estate papers.

Ozias Polkinghorne did own a mill. It was Brackenholt Mill, on his own home farm, on the other side of the county. He never owned Cauldmere. The source line said so, in small grey letters under the answer. Nobody reads the small grey letters at two in the morning.
The archive had given a dead man's widow a mill he never owned, and shown its working underneath.

Cauldmere Mill is in the Wyvenhall estate papers. Its name appears once, in the document's header: deeds and leases of Cauldmere Mill. Every page after that calls it "the said mill". So does every page of the Polkinghorne papers, and of the Gorsedene rentals. On Saturday I reran the question with the search log on and drew the five chunks it sent.

Middle row: rank 4, G3, Gorsedene 1885, the mill empty, 0.03077; rank 5, P3, Polkinghorne accounts of 1866, a new wheel, 0.03055. Bottom: the reply at 02:14, the widow, answered from rank 1.

blocks.caption: Saturday's rerun, from the search log. The five chunks sent, by fused score (BM25 and the embedding, joined by rank fusion): P2, the Polkinghorne will of January 1871, 0.03279 (BM25 3.00, cosine 0.50); G2, the Gorsedene rent for 1871, 0.03226; W3, the Wyvenhall sale of March 1871 to the tenant, Jethro Rosewarne, 0.03175 (BM25 1.28, cosine 0.41); G3, 0.03077; P3, 0.03055. Not one of the five contains the word Cauldmere. For "and after her?" every chunk scored 0.00.

blocks.text: The visitor wrote to the office on Monday; her message is below. The assistant goes back on before the family history fair. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your strongroom is haunted, though I'd keep the lights on. What you did on Saturday has a name: a retrieval log, a record of each question as it was searched, the chunks that came back and their scores. Keep one for every question, always; it's where debugging starts. Two questions. Take W3, the sale to Rosewarne: what text, word for word, went into its embedding and its keyword index? And when the visitor typed "and after her?", what words were left for the search to use?

replies.author: u/strongroom_ursula
replies.text: W3, word for word: "1871. In March Sir Ebenezer sold the said mill to his tenant, Jethro Rosewarne, for 1,100 pounds." That's all. The estate and section sit beside it as metadata; they go under the answer and nowhere else. Cauldmere isn't in any chunk's text. For the follow-up: keyword search drops stop words, the little words like and, after and her, and that left nothing at all. Every score was 0.00.

comments.author: u/just_upgrade_it_keverne
comments.text: The embedding model is the problem. You're on a small general model that has never seen an 1870s deed; to it, sold to his tenant and passed to his widow are just two sentences about property. Switch to a better one, one of the big new models, re-embed the archive over a weekend, and it will know which chunk belongs to which mill. Everything else is fiddling.

replies.author: u/strongroom_ursula
replies.text: A weekend I can find. The office would rather pay for a model than for my overtime.

replies.author: u/just_upgrade_it_keverne
replies.text: Then it's settled. Better vectors, better answers.

comments.author: u/millrace_wenonah
comments.text: I was the visitor. Jethro Rosewarne was my great-great-grandfather. He rented Cauldmere Mill from the Wyvenhall estate from 1858 and bought it in March 1871; we still have his copy of the deed. When he died it went to his son Lemuel, and it burned in 1902. Nobody called Polkinghorne ever owned it. I asked who came after her because I thought your archive knew part of the story we'd lost. It's a strange feeling, being told your family's mill went to a stranger's widow.

replies.author: u/strongroom_ursula
replies.text: W3 is his deed. That night it came third, and it was sent. I'm sorry, and I'll write to you when it's fixed.

reply.prompt: The office wants the night assistant back on before the family history fair in November. What should Ursula change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise top-k from 5 to 20, so the right chunk is always among the passages that the model gets to read.
options.part2: I raised top-k from 5 to 20. In the archive that sends four times the passage tokens, 6,000 a question against 1,500; in my test sample of 12 chunks it sends all 12. I asked again: who owned Cauldmere Mill in 1871? The top chunk was still the Polkinghorne will, P2, at 0.03279, and the answer still gave the mill to the widow. W3, the real sale, had been in the five all along, third; now it sat among eleven others, and still nothing in its text said Cauldmere. "And after her?" still scored 0.00 everywhere. On the eight known questions I wrote on Saturday, the right chunk reached the model for 6 and the answer was right for 4, exactly as before.
options.senior: More chunks help when the right one is missing from the list. Here it was already sent, third, and lost because nothing in its text tied it to the question. Read the log before touching k: if the right chunk is there and still not used, the fault is in what the chunk says. Anthropic's tests did find 20 chunks worked better than 5 or 10, but in a setup where every chunk already carried its context.

options.text: Switch to a better embedding model and re-embed the whole archive; this one does not understand old deeds.
options.verdict: A better reader of the same words
options.part2: We switched to a bigger embedding model and re-embedded all 31,400 chunks over a weekend; in my test sample its stand-in counts related words together, owned with bought, sold and passed. The Polkinghorne will still came first, 0.03227, with W3 just behind at 0.03200, and the answer still gave Cauldmere Mill to the widow. The new model liked G3 best of all, the Gorsedene note that the mill stood empty and the woods were sold, 0.71 on its own list: it judges what a chunk is about better, and no chunk is about Cauldmere. "And after her?" found nothing. Known questions: 6 and 4, unchanged.
options.senior: A better embedding model reads the same text better; it can't read text that isn't there. The mill's name lived only in the header, so no model could place W3 nearer a question about Cauldmere than the widow's chunk. Change the model when the log shows it misjudging what a chunk says, and measure the change on the known questions before paying for it.

options.text: Have volunteers label every chunk by hand with its estate and mill, so that none just says the said mill.
options.part2: Two volunteers and I started labelling: each chunk's text gets its estate and mill in front, such as Wyvenhall estate, Cauldmere Mill. At 30 seconds a chunk, 31,400 chunks is about 262 hours, 131 of my nights at two hours each. We did the three estates in my test sample first and asked again. W3 came first, 0.03252, from the Wyvenhall estate papers, and the answer named Jethro Rosewarne. "And after her?" still found nothing. Known questions: right chunk in the top k 6 of 8, answered right 5 of 8. And new deposits arrive every month, unlabelled.
options.senior: Putting each document's name into its chunks' text is the right idea, and doing it by hand is the slowest way to do it, and easy to get wrong on chunk 20,000. It also leaves follow-ups broken, because the question itself has no words to search with. Let a model write the context from each document, check a sample by hand, and fix follow-ups separately.

options.text: Read failed searches, let a model add each document's context to its chunks, rewrite follow-ups, test.
options.part2: I kept the log on for every question. Then each chunk got its document's context written in front of its text before embedding and indexing: a model reads the document and writes one line per chunk, such as From the Wyvenhall estate papers: deeds and leases of Cauldmere Mill, 1846 to 1902. For the archive that is 31,400 model calls, about $12.75 once at Anthropic's published estimate. Follow-ups are rewritten as standalone questions from the conversation before the search. The night again: W3 first, 0.03252 (BM25 2.36, cosine 0.58), from the Wyvenhall estate papers. "And after her?" became "who owned Cauldmere Mill after Jethro Rosewarne?" and found W4: his son, Lemuel. Known questions: right chunk in the top k 8 of 8, answered right 7 of 8. The miss was "who bought Brackenholt Mill in 1880?": the papers say sold, not bought, and the answer came from the 1866 accounts for a new wheel. Embedding a hypothetical answer instead of the question, HyDE, closed it, 8 of 8, at one more model call a question.
options.senior: Debug retrieval in order: read what was retrieved, find why the right chunk lost, fix that cause, and measure on known questions. Here the chunk lost because the words that mattered lived only in the header, so the context goes into the searched text, not only beside it. The follow-up lost because it had no words, so it is rewritten first. Each fix has a price: a model call per chunk once, a call per question to rewrite, another for HyDE.

sim.title: Debug the Fenmarrow night assistant
sim.lede: You're Ursula on Saturday, rerunning the night with the retrieval log on. There is no real model and no real embedding. The sim holds a teaching sample of 12 chunks from three estates' papers: W1 to W4 from the Wyvenhall papers (Cauldmere Mill), P1 to P4 from the Polkinghorne papers (Brackenholt Mill) and G1 to G4 from the Gorsedene rentals (Sallowford fulling mill). Every body chunk says "the said mill"; each mill's name is only in its document's header and in the metadata shown under answers. The search is hybrid. BM25 (k1 1.2, b 0.75) scores each chunk's words, with stop words such as and, after and her dropped. A stand-in embedding counts 28 listed keywords and compares the counts by cosine; it exaggerates, because a chunk with none of the listed words scores 0.00 where a real embedding would only score low. The two ranked lists are joined by reciprocal rank fusion, k = 60, and equal fused scores go to the better BM25 rank. A stand-in answerer reads the top k and answers from the first chunk whose text names the mill asked about, or else the first chunk, writing the asked mill's name in place of "the said mill". Document context puts a one-line description of the chunk's document into its text before indexing; hand labels put the estate and mill there instead. Query rewriting turns a follow-up into a standalone question, one that makes sense on its own, using the person the previous answer named. HyDE, hypothetical document embeddings, embeds a stated hypothetical answer in place of the question on the vector side. The better embedding model is a stand-in that also counts related words together, owned with bought, sold and passed. Below the night's two questions are eight known questions with their right chunks. The archive's other 31,388 chunks are assumed to rank below these 12: a teaching assumption.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the night, top 5 and nothing on. P2, the Polkinghorne will, is first at 0.03279 and the answer gives Cauldmere Mill to the widow; W3, the real sale, is third at 0.03175; "and after her?" scores 0.00 everywhere. Known set: right chunk in the top k 6 of 8, answered right 4 of 8. Pick Top-k 20: the same answers, at 6,000 passage tokens a question. Pick Better embedding model: P2 at 0.03227 still beats W3 at 0.03200, and G3 jumps to first on the vector side. Go back to the night and turn on Query rewriting alone: the follow-up becomes "who owned Cauldmere Mill after Petronella Polkinghorne?" and the widow comes back again. Pick Context, rewriting, known set: W3 first at 0.03252, the follow-up finds W4, 8 of 8 and 7 of 8. Read the one miss, then turn on HyDE: 8 of 8, at 3 model calls a question.

explain.oneLine: Nothing forged the record. Each mill's name lived only in its document's header, shown under answers but never embedded or indexed, so the widow's chunk won on the words it shared with the question, and a follow-up with no nouns found nothing at all.

steps.title: Read what was retrieved, first.
steps.text: Before changing anything, look at the retrieval log: the question as searched, the chunks that came back, their scores, and which one the answer used. It tells you which kind of failure you have. If the right chunk is missing, retrieval missed it. If it's there and loses, ask why it lost. If every score is zero, the question has nothing to search with. Ursula's log showed all three questions at once: W3, the real sale, came third at 0.03175 and was sent, the answer came from P2 at 0.03279, and the follow-up scored 0.00 everywhere.

steps.title: Metadata shown is not text searched.
steps.text: The bookbinder's case taught to keep each chunk's section path as metadata and show it under the answer, and the archive did exactly that. It still failed, because the search compares the question with each chunk's text, and only its text. The word Cauldmere was in a header and in a metadata field, never in a chunk. So the question's one distinctive word matched nothing, and the ranking fell back on the words it did share, owned, mill and 1871: P2 holds all three, W3 only two. Showing the source let a careful reader catch the error; it couldn't stop it.

steps.title: Contextual retrieval puts the context into the text.
steps.text: Anthropic's contextual retrieval has a model read the whole document and write a short context for each chunk, usually 50 to 100 tokens, which is put in front of the chunk before it is embedded and before the BM25 index is built. Now W3's searched text begins From the Wyvenhall estate papers: deeds and leases of Cauldmere Mill. In the sim it comes first at 0.03252. The price is one model call per chunk, once, and again whenever a document changes; prompt caching keeps it down, because the document is loaded once and reused for each of its chunks. Anthropic puts it at $1.02 per million document tokens, about $12.75 for the archive's 12.5 million.

steps.title: Follow-ups have no words: rewrite them.
steps.text: The model keeps no memory between requests, so the app sends the conversation history; but the search sees only the latest message. "And after her?" is all stop words. Query rewriting has a model turn it into a standalone question first, using the conversation: who owned Cauldmere Mill after Jethro Rosewarne? That finds W4. The catch is in the sim: with the first answer still wrong, the rewrite becomes after Petronella Polkinghorne and fetches the widow again. Fix the retrieval before the rewriter, and log the rewritten question, not only the typed one.

steps.title: HyDE for wording gaps, and measure every change.
steps.text: With context and rewriting, 7 of the 8 known questions were answered right. The miss asked who bought Brackenholt Mill in 1880; the papers say sold. HyDE, from Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan's paper Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels, has a model write a hypothetical answer and embeds that instead, so the search compares document with document. It closed the miss, at a model call per question, and the made-up answer can carry false details. Every change here was judged the same way: on the same eight questions, counting right chunks in the top k and right answers separately.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as Ursula rebuilt it. Left column: the Wyvenhall papers, whose header names Cauldmere Mill, and below it the metadata, estate and section, which is only shown under answers. Middle column: a context line written once per chunk that names Cauldmere Mill, and below it W3's own text, which says the said mill. Both the context line and W3's text go into the embedding and the BM25 index, on the right. The question, rewritten if it is a follow-up, searches that index, and the answer comes from W3, with the metadata shown under it.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn as Ursula rebuilt it. The header's words reach the search only through the context line, which sits in front of W3's own text in both the embedding and the BM25 index; the metadata, estate and section, is still shown under the answer and still never searched. A follow-up is rewritten as a standalone question before it searches. The night comes back W3 first at 0.03252, the follow-up finds W4, and the eight known questions run before every change: 8 of 8 in the top k, 7 of 8 right.

fix.title: The fix: log every search, put context in the text, rewrite follow-ups, and measure
fix.text: Keep a retrieval log for every question: the question as searched, the chunks, their scores and the one the answer used. Have a model write a one-line context for each chunk from its whole document and put it in front of the chunk's text before embedding and before the BM25 index; keep the original text and the context as separate fields, so the context can be checked and written again. Rewrite each follow-up as a standalone question from the conversation before searching, and log the rewrite. Keep a set of known questions, including follow-ups, and run it before and after every change. On Ursula's eight, this took the night from 4 right to 7; HyDE, at a model call a question, took it to 8.

limits: The context is only as good as the document it is written from. A page filed in the wrong bundle gets the wrong bundle's context, and then the wrong label is in the searched text itself. Check a sample of the generated lines against the catalogue, and rerun them whenever documents move or change.

Rewriting inherits the conversation's mistakes: with the first answer wrong, the rewrite searched for the widow again. Rewrites can also drop exact terms; Microsoft's Azure AI Search page warns that rewritten queries might not contain all of the exact terms the original query had. Log both versions.

HyDE adds a model call and some latency to every question, and its hypothetical answer may contain false details, as its authors say. And for a small enough collection you may not need retrieval at all: Anthropic notes that a knowledge base under about 200,000 tokens can simply go in the prompt.

explain.seniorTake: When a RAG system answers wrongly, the retrieval is usually where it went wrong, and the log is where you find out how. Look at what came back before you change anything: missing, outranked, or nothing to search with are three different faults with three different fixes. Many outranked chunks lose for the same reason, that the words which make them relevant live somewhere the search can't see, in a title, a header or a metadata field. Put that context into the searched text, make every question standalone before it searches, reach for HyDE when the question and the documents use different words, and judge each change on the same known questions, counting retrieval and answers separately. A bigger model or a bigger k feels like progress and rarely is, when the text never held the answer's key word.

realWorld.title: Anthropic, 2024: chunks lose their context
realWorld.text: Anthropic's post Introducing Contextual Retrieval (19 September 2024) says traditional RAG solutions remove context when encoding information. Its example is a chunk saying a company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter, which on its own doesn't specify which company it's referring to or the relevant time period. That is the said mill, in a filing instead of a deed.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: context before embedding and BM25
realWorld.text: The post describes prepending chunk-specific explanatory context to each chunk before embedding, and before creating the BM25 index, with a model asked to give a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document. It says the resulting contextual text is usually 50 to 100 tokens.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: failed retrievals down 35%, 49% and 67%
realWorld.text: Measuring failure as 1 minus recall@20, the post reports that contextual embeddings reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% to 3.7%), contextual embeddings with contextual BM25 by 49% (to 2.9%), and the two with reranking added by 67% (to 1.9%).

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the cost, with prompt caching
realWorld.text: With prompt caching, the post says, you simply load the document into the cache once and then reference the previously cached content, and it puts the one-time cost to generate contextualized chunks at $1.02 per million document tokens. It also found top-20 the most performant of 5, 10 and 20 chunks, adding that it is worth experimenting on your use case.

realWorld.title: Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan, 2022: HyDE
realWorld.text: Luyu Gao, Xueguang Ma, Jimmy Lin and Jamie Callan's Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (arXiv 2212.10496, December 2022) proposes Hypothetical Document Embeddings: an instruction-following language model (e.g. InstructGPT) writes a hypothetical document for the query, and an unsupervised encoder embeds it to find similar real documents.

realWorld.title: HyDE: a made-up document, filtered by the encoder
realWorld.text: The abstract is frank about the trade: the document captures relevance patterns but is unreal and may contain false details, with the encoder's dense bottleneck filtering out the incorrect details, and the second step grounds it to the actual corpus. The authors report it significantly outperforms the unsupervised retriever Contriever.

realWorld.title: Azure AI Search: query rewriting, in preview
realWorld.text: Microsoft's page Rewrite Queries with Semantic Ranker describes query rewriting (preview) as transforming a user's query into a more effective one: the service sends the query to a generative model that generates alternative queries, and searches with the original and the rewrites. queryRewrites set to generative|count-5 asks for up to five; the count can be 1 to 10.

asked: Your RAG answers are wrong: how do you debug it?
How do you handle follow-up questions in a RAG chat?
interview.answer: I start with the retrieval log, not the model: for each failing question, what was searched, which chunks came back with what scores, and which one the answer used. That sorts the failure. If the right chunk isn't retrieved, it's a retrieval problem; if it's retrieved and outranked, I ask why; if every score is near zero, the question has nothing to search with. A common cause of outranking is that the deciding words live outside the chunk, in a document title or header kept only as metadata. Contextual retrieval fixes that: a model writes a short context for each chunk from its document, 50 to 100 tokens in Anthropic's version, and it goes in front of the chunk before embedding and keyword indexing; with prompt caching the one-time cost is small. Follow-ups like and after her? get rewritten into standalone questions from the conversation history before searching, and I log the rewrite, because a rewrite can carry an earlier wrong answer forward. Where questions and documents use different words, HyDE, embedding a hypothetical answer, can help at a model call per query. Every change gets measured on a fixed set of known questions, including follow-ups, counting right chunks retrieved and right answers separately.

terms.def: An archivist who works the night shift. Ursula keeps the Fenmarrow Record Office's search room and its overnight assistant.
The room in a record office where visitors read documents. Fenmarrow's is empty after six; its assistant answers online overnight.
A locked, fire-resistant store where an archive keeps its original documents.
The records of a landed estate: deeds, leases, wills, rentals and accounts, often given to a county record office in bundles.
Here, the title at the top of a document, such as deeds and leases of Cauldmere Mill. Each Fenmarrow document names its mill only there.
Old legal wording for the mill already named earlier in the document. It is why no body chunk carries the mill's own name.
A signed legal document that transfers or records ownership of property, such as the sale of Cauldmere Mill in 1871.
An agreement that lets someone use property for a set time in return for rent. The tenant is the one renting.
A document saying who should receive a person's property when they die. P2 records Ozias Polkinghorne's.
A mill that cleaned and thickened woollen cloth by pounding it in water. The person who ran one was a fuller.
An estate's record of the rents its tenants paid. The Gorsedene papers are rentals.
Two old English quarter days when rents were often due: Lady Day on 25 March, Michaelmas on 29 September.
A low barrier across a river that raises the water to drive a mill wheel.
A batch of papers given to a record office. New deposits arrive at Fenmarrow every month.
Facts stored about a chunk beside its text, such as its estate and section. Fenmarrow shows them under answers; they are not searched.
A record, per question, of the query as searched, the chunks returned, their scores and the chunk the answer used. Where debugging retrieval starts.
Very common words, such as and, after and her, that keyword search usually drops. A question made only of them leaves nothing to search with.
The text of a chunk that is actually embedded and indexed for keyword search. In the sim's table, the text searched column.
A short line describing the document a chunk comes from, put in front of the chunk's text before indexing, so the chunk is searchable by what the document is about.
Anthropic's 2024 method: a model writes a short context for each chunk from the whole document, put in front of the chunk before embedding and before building the BM25 index.
The two halves of contextual retrieval: embedding each chunk with its context in front, and building the keyword index from the same text.
The sim's stated document context, one per document, such as From the Wyvenhall estate papers: deeds and leases of Cauldmere Mill, 1846 to 1902.
The sim's version of labelling by hand: the estate and mill, such as Wyvenhall estate, Cauldmere Mill, typed in front of each chunk's text.
A question that depends on the conversation before it, such as and after her? On its own it often has no words worth searching for.
A question that makes sense on its own, without the conversation: who owned Cauldmere Mill after Jethro Rosewarne?
Changing a question before searching, for example turning a follow-up into a standalone question using the conversation. Usually done by a model call.
Hypothetical document embeddings: a model writes a made-up answer to the question, and the search embeds that answer instead of the question.
The made-up answer HyDE embeds. It may be wrong in its details; it is used only to find real documents that look like it.
This lab's script in place of an embedding model: it counts 28 stated keywords in a text and compares counts by cosine. It exaggerates: no shared keyword scores 0.00.
How many times each word on a fixed list appears in a text. A word counts when it starts with the keyword, so owned counts for own.
The sim's stand-in for a bigger model: it also counts passed, kept, inherit and held, and puts related words such as owned, bought and sold on one position.
The sim's script in place of the model: it answers from the first sent chunk whose text names the mill asked about, else the first, writing that mill's name for the said mill.
In the sim, chunks with equal fused scores are ordered by the better BM25 rank, then by chunk order. Real systems may break ties differently.
Ursula's eight test questions with their right chunks marked, including two follow-ups. Every change is run against all eight.

terms.term: Right chunk in the top k
terms.def: How many known questions had their right chunk among the top k sent. It says the chunk arrived, not that the answer used it.
How many known questions were answered from their right chunk. Counted separately from the right chunk in the top k.
The tokens of the chunks sent to the model with a question. Fenmarrow's chunks are about 300 tokens, so top 5 is about 1,500.
One request to a language model. Rewriting and HyDE each add one per question; writing context adds one per chunk, once.
The tokens in the documents being processed, the unit of Anthropic's cost estimate for writing context. Fenmarrow's papers come to about 12.5 million.
The share of test questions whose right chunk is not retrieved. Anthropic measured it as 1 minus recall@20, within the top 20 chunks.
A language model tuned to follow written instructions. InstructGPT is the HyDE paper's example.
A model that turns text into a vector. In HyDE, an encoder trained without labelled examples embeds the hypothetical document.
Vector search with an embedding model that was never trained on labelled question and answer pairs for the task: the setting HyDE was built for.
Human judgements of which documents answer which questions, used to train or test search. HyDE needs none.
The paper's phrase for squeezing a whole document into one fixed-length vector, which loses fine details, including some false ones.
An embedding model for search trained without labelled pairs, which the HyDE paper calls an unsupervised retriever and compares against.
Microsoft's hosted search service, with keyword, vector and hybrid search. Query rewriting runs with its semantic ranker.
A cloud feature offered before general release, usually without a service-level agreement and liable to change.
A model that writes new text, such as a language model, as opposed to one that only scores or embeds text.
An internal assistant that answers staff questions from company policies, such as leave, travel or expenses.
The clause of ISO 9001 on controlling documented information, including that it is available and suitable for use where and when it is needed.
The international standard for quality management systems. Companies are certified against it by outside auditors.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that answers from many similar documents: a policy assistant, a contracts search, a support bot over product manuals. A common incident: a policy assistant tells a contractor they may carry over ten days of leave, because every policy's chunks say the employee may, the leave policy for permanent staff outranked the contractor policy, and the policy's name lived only in its title and metadata. The team fixed it the way Ursula did: they turned on a retrieval log, saw the right chunk sitting fourth, put each policy's name and scope in front of every chunk before embedding and keyword indexing, rewrote follow-ups such as what about part-timers? into standalone questions, and checked it all on twenty known questions written by the policy owners. Look at your own chunks: does each one say, in its own text, which document and version it comes from? Is every search logged with its chunks and scores? Standards-readiness note: if your company holds or is pursuing ISO 9001:2015 certification, clause 7.5.3 asks that documented information be available and suitable for use where and when it is needed; an assistant that answers from the wrong policy is the kind of gap an auditor raises, so build the retrieval log and the known questions in from the first release rather than at audit time. In the crossover season, Nightwatch's Build Night X1 builds an incident copilot with RAG over runbooks; give each runbook chunk the runbook's name and its alarm in its text, not only in its metadata.

recall.prompt: Your company's support bot answers from 400 product manuals, chunked and embedded. A customer asks whether the K40 kettle's base fits the K20, and gets an answer about a different model. Every chunk says this unit; the model number is only in each manual's title, which your pipeline stores as metadata and shows under the answer. The log shows the right chunk came 9th. A teammate wants a bigger embedding model. What do you tell them, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The model number never reaches the search: it is only in the title and metadata, not in the embedded or indexed chunk text
Put each manual's context, such as its title and model number, in front of every chunk before embedding and keyword indexing: contextual retrieval
Check the change on known questions, counting retrieved chunks and right answers, before shipping it

recall.model: I'd tell them a bigger embedding model reads the same text better, but the model number isn't in the text: every chunk says this unit, and the K40 lives only in the manual's title, which is stored as metadata and shown under the answer but never embedded or indexed. So no embedding can tie the right chunk to the question. I'd put each manual's context, its title, model number and section, in front of every chunk before embedding and building the keyword index, which is contextual retrieval, written by a model from each manual once. Then I'd measure it on known questions with their right chunks marked, including a few that name a model number, counting whether the right chunk is retrieved and whether the answer used it, and keep the retrieval log on.

recall.prompt: What does contextual retrieval change in a RAG pipeline?
options: It sends every earlier turn of the chat to the search engine along with the question.
It stores each chunk's document title as metadata and shows it under the answer.
It puts a short context about the chunk's document in front of each chunk's text before embedding and keyword indexing.
It replaces the embedding model with one trained on the company's own documents.
recall.why: Contextual retrieval changes what is searched. A model writes a short context for each chunk from its whole document, 50 to 100 tokens in Anthropic's version, and that context goes in front of the chunk before it is embedded and before the BM25 index is built. Keeping the title as metadata and showing it is useful for checking sources, but it is never searched, which is exactly how the Fenmarrow assistant failed.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: a user asks a RAG chatbot about a policy, gets a good answer, then types and for contractors? and gets nothing useful. Why, and how do you handle follow-up questions in a RAG chat?

keyIdeas.idea: The search only sees the latest message, which on its own lacks the subject: it has nothing distinctive to search with
Rewrite the follow-up into a standalone question using the conversation history before searching
Log the rewritten query and test follow-ups, because rewriting costs a call and can carry an earlier wrong answer forward

recall.model: The search only sees the latest message, and and for contractors? on its own has no subject; the policy name is in an earlier turn, so the retriever has almost nothing to match. I'd rewrite every follow-up into a standalone question before searching, with a model call that reads the conversation history and writes, say, what is the leave policy for contractors? Then I'd log both the typed and the rewritten query, because a rewrite can carry an earlier wrong answer forward or drop an exact term, and it adds a model call and some latency per message. And I'd add follow-up pairs to the test set, so every change is checked on them too.

recall.prompt: What does HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings) do, and what does it cost?
options: It embeds each document twice with two models and averages them; it doubles storage.
A model writes a hypothetical answer to the question, and that answer is embedded and searched instead of the question; it costs a model call per query.
It labels every document by hand with a hypothetical title; it costs reviewer time.
It asks the user to write an example answer before searching; it costs nothing.
recall.why: HyDE, from Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan's 2022 paper, has an instruction-following model write a hypothetical document for the query and embeds that, so the search compares a document-shaped text with documents. The paper says the hypothetical document may contain false details, which the encoder partly filters out. The cost is a model call, and its latency, on every query.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Context lines, rewriting and the log ran all winter. The known questions grew to 40 and 39 came back right. Then a researcher asked what repairs were made to Cauldmere Mill, and the assistant answered: a new wheel, 140 pounds, in 1866, source Wyvenhall estate papers. That entry is Brackenholt's, from the Polkinghorne accounts. When I pulled the box, twelve pages of Polkinghorne accounts had been scanned inside the Wyvenhall bundle years ago. The search log shows the wheel chunk's text now starts From the Wyvenhall estate papers: deeds and leases of Cauldmere Mill. The label is forged, and this time it's inside the chunk.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did a Polkinghorne page come back as Cauldmere, and what do you change so it can't happen quietly again?

keyIdeas.idea: The context line is written from the document a chunk sits in, so misfiled pages inherited the Wyvenhall document's context, and the wrong label is now in the searched text
Refile the pages and write their context again; keep the original text and the context as separate fields so affected chunks can be found and regenerated
Check generated context against the catalogue, spot-check samples, and add known questions for this kind of mix-up

coldCase.model: The context line is written by a model from the document each chunk belongs to, and as far as the pipeline knew, those twelve Polkinghorne pages belonged to the Wyvenhall bundle. So they inherited the Wyvenhall context, Cauldmere Mill and all, and the wrong label went into the searched text itself, where it now helps the wrong chunk win. Refile the pages in the catalogue and write their context again from the right document. Keep the original text and the context as separate fields, with the document each context came from, so you can find every chunk a bad bundle touched and regenerate just those. Then add a check: compare each generated context with the catalogue entry for its pages and flag any mismatch, spot-check a sample of new context lines by hand, and add known questions for repairs and other entries that look alike across estates.
